---
title: "Why a bigger plate makes you eat more"
description: "The same portion looks small on a large plate and generous on a small one. Your eyes decide how full you are before your stomach gets a say."
image: /assets/social/why-a-bigger-plate-makes-you-eat-more-og.png
author: "Mesfin Genie"
date: "2026-08-16"
categories: [behavioural economics, health, everyday]
---

Put a normal portion on a large dinner plate and it looks meagre. Put the
same portion on a small plate and it looks like plenty. Nothing about the
food changed. Your judgement of how much you are eating did.

This is an old visual illusion with a name, and it has a very practical
consequence: people served on bigger plates take more, eat more, and report
feeling no fuller. The eye estimates the portion against the rim, and the rim
lies.

The effect is not large per meal. It is large across a year, because it
happens at every meal, and because the correction goes only one way. A small
plate never makes you feel you have overeaten.

I like this example because the usual advice about eating is about
willpower, and this has nothing to do with willpower. It is a fact about
perception, and you can change the plate instead of trying to change
yourself. That is the general shape of a good nudge: alter the environment
so that the easy choice and the better choice are the same one, and leave
the person's freedom exactly where it was.

If you want to eat a bit less, do not buy a book. Buy smaller plates.
